evidence_items.title: Individual lament and the collective epilogue in Psalm 25
evidence_items.description: Psalm 25 moves through an alphabetically organized individual prayer and ends with a separate petition for Israel; the relation of that final verse to the poem’s original composition is uncertain.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The acrostic frame, individual petitions, and explicit appeal for Israel can be observed in the Hebrew text. Human describes verse 22 as an epilogue and notes that its status as a later addition is possible, not established.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Helps readers follow how personal distress and instruction broaden into a communal plea without assuming the final verse’s date or redactional history.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 25 is an alphabetic acrostic prayer with first-person petitions and reflections through vv. 1–21; v. 22 shifts to an explicit plea to redeem Israel. The final verse sits outside the preceding individual address and sequence.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Human reads vv. 1–21 primarily as an individual lament and describes v. 22 as an epilogue that extends the worshipper’s experience to Israel. He allows that the verse may be a later addition, while other structural descriptions place the boundary differently. The text’s acrostic form does not by itself establish its date or original use.

periods: Ancient Israelite acrostic prayer; composition date and compositional history unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: An individual voice asks for guidance, forgiveness, and deliverance before a final communal appeal for Israel.
temporal_scope.notes: The possible secondary status of v. 22 is Human’s proposal, not a settled textual or redactional finding.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The contrast between the individual prayer through v. 21 and the explicit communal petition in v. 22 requires the full poem.

evidence_items.title: Cush the Benjaminite and the limits of a Davidic setting
evidence_items.description: Psalm 7’s superscription names Cush the Benjaminite, but the poem does not independently identify a person or event; proposed links to David’s conflicts remain reconstructions.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The superscription and the poem’s danger language are explicit. Berger offers a specific Saul-flight proposal in an abstract-only source; Obiorah documents an alternative ancient-version reading and cautions that a proposed Absalom-death setting does not fit the poem’s threat language.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Helps readers distinguish the received superscription from an independently recoverable episode and see why historical identification remains unsettled.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The superscription associates the shiggaion with David and “the words of Cush, a Benjaminite.” The speaker asks for rescue from pursuers and describes life-threatening danger, but the poem itself names no encounter in Samuel.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Berger argues that the superscription invites comparison with a wider set of Samuel narratives in which David restrains himself toward Saul and other Benjaminites; the abstract places the Cush episode during David’s flight from Saul and relates the poem to 1 Samuel 24 and 1 Chronicles 12. Obiorah reports that some ancient Greek and other versions read “Cushite,” prompting a proposed link to the messenger announcing Absalom’s death in 2 Samuel 18; she judges the poem’s threat language a poor fit for a dirge. These are competing reconstructions, not independently verified biographies. Berger’s full article was not accessible.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A superscription attributes the prayer to David and names Cush the Benjaminite; the poem describes pursuit but supplies no independently identified episode.
temporal_scope.notes: The Saul-flight and Absalom-messenger settings are distinct scholarly proposals. The superscription does not establish a composition date or a named historical event.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The superscription and full poem must be read together to assess whether the title identifies a recoverable event.

evidence_items.title: Refuge and spatial rhetoric in Psalm 11
evidence_items.description: Psalm 11 places advice to flee alongside the speaker’s confession of refuge in YHWH and an image of YHWH enthroned in the holy temple.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The poem’s movement between flight, refuge, the temple/heavenly throne, and the upright seeing YHWH is textually observable. Prinsloo’s explanation of this movement as a spatial representation of suffering and restored presence is an attributed literary reading.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how the poem answers counsel to flee and gives its language of trust a spatial and theological shape without reconstructing a specific temple ceremony.
evidence_items.primary_observation: One voice asks why the speaker should flee like a bird; the speaker instead confesses refuge in YHWH. The poem locates YHWH in the holy temple and on a heavenly throne, then closes with the upright seeing YHWH’s face.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Prinsloo reads the poem through movement between “off-centre” danger and “at-centre” refuge: the hunted righteous are threatened, while YHWH’s temple and heavenly throne provide the poem’s center of judgment and presence. He interprets the final restoration language as a spatial answer to suffering and social dislocation. This is a literary account of the poem’s rhetoric, not a description of a recoverable worship rite.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A confession of trust answers advice to flee and imagines YHWH as judge in the temple and heavenly throne room.
temporal_scope.notes: The spatial reading concerns the poem’s imagery and does not date its composition or identify a particular historical crisis.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The whole poem develops the contrast between flight, refuge, YHWH’s throne, and the upright’s final presence before YHWH.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 53 as a revised form of Psalm 14: a redactional proposal
evidence_items.description: Psalm 53 repeats much of Psalm 14 with deliberate differences; Botha argues that the later-form poem adapts Psalm 14 to its position among Psalms 52–55.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The substantial shared wording and differences are directly observable. Botha’s proposed direction of revision and explanation from the Psalter’s present arrangement are scholarly interpretations; alternative direction proposals are part of the debate.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Helps readers notice how a repeated poem can be reshaped for a new literary setting while keeping textual observation distinct from a reconstruction of editorial history.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 14 and Psalm 53 share most of their sequence and wording but differ at several points, including how the wicked are described and the formulation of their terror and fate. Their divine-name usage also reflects the Psalter’s Elohistic collection.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Botha argues that Psalm 53 is an intentional adaptation of Psalm 14, revised for its current place among Psalms 52–55 and its wisdom-oriented reading of David’s story. He acknowledges the reverse proposal—that Psalm 14 developed from Psalm 53—but rejects it as a less adequate explanation of the differences. The text establishes close literary reuse; it does not by itself establish when, by whom, or in which direction the poems were first composed. No cross-passage relationship edge is authored here.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A closely related pair of poems appears in different locations in the Psalter; Psalm 53 sits among Psalms 52–55.
temporal_scope.notes: Botha’s direction-of-dependence and editorial-setting claims are proposals. The CKL anchor and reader route remain limited to Psalm 14.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The seven-verse poem contains the wording and variations at issue; Psalm 53 is discussed as a comparison, not authored as a separate Scripture route.

evidence_items.title: Text-critical proposals at Psalm 17:11 and 17:14
evidence_items.description: A recent text-critical study accepts a conjectural reading at Psalm 17:11 and prefers the Masoretic qere at 17:14; neither decision should be mistaken for a settled original reading.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The English abstract reports the author’s preferred readings but does not provide the full Italian argument. One reading is explicitly conjectural, and the other is a preference between Masoretic forms; no claim about the original text is made.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Lets readers see where translation depends on text-critical judgment and separates a conjecture from an attested reading tradition.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The article identifies textual and translation difficulties at its verses 11 and 14. Its abstract reports a conjectural reading at v. 11, “they have advanced against me; now they have encircled me,” and prefers the qere וּצְפוּנְךָ at v. 14, understood collectively as “your protected ones.”
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Bazyliński’s abstract presents both as editorial judgments: the first is a conjecture, while the second prefers the qere reading. The English abstract does not expose the article’s full comparison of Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions, so the item records the proposals without claiming which wording is earliest or original. The full article text is in Italian and was not reviewed.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: An individual prayer whose wording at two points has been treated as textually or translationally difficult.
temporal_scope.notes: The English abstract is the consulted portion. A conjectural emendation, the Masoretic qere/ketiv distinction, and the date of any manuscript witness are separate questions.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The full prayer contains both locations discussed in the article; no single reading is promoted as the original.

evidence_items.title: The unusual “request” term in Psalm 21:2
evidence_items.description: One published proposal reads the unusual word for the king’s “request” as an echo of diplomatic correspondence; the accessible abstract alone does not establish borrowing.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Sheveka’s abstract explicitly proposes a parallel with Amarna correspondence but the full article and its primary-text analysis were not accessible. The psalm’s unusual term is observable; the historical-literary connection remains a proposal.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Highlights a lexical feature in the royal petition and shows how a court-trained audience might hear diplomatic register without treating that reconstruction as a fact.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 21:2 says that the king’s request was not withheld. Sheveka’s abstract identifies the Hebrew noun for “request” as a hapax legomenon and compares the phrase with diplomatic correspondence in Amarna Letter EA 9.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Sheveka proposes that the expression evokes the formal “brotherhood” relation between equal kings and that court scribes adapted diplomatic language for a king’s address to God. This is a specific lexical-historical proposal, not proof that the psalm was composed in a royal chancery or that it directly borrowed EA 9. The article’s full text and underlying letter discussion were not accessible.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A royal thanksgiving says the king’s request was granted; no ruler or historical occasion is named.
temporal_scope.notes: The proposed EA 9 echo is attributed to Sheveka and based here only on the abstract. The Amarna letter’s date, the psalm’s date, and possible transmission are not established.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The unusual noun translated “request” appears in this single verse and is the focus of the abstract-level lexical proposal.

evidence_items.title: Walking in integrity and wisdom-shaped structure in Psalm 26
evidence_items.description: Psalm 26 repeats the language of walking in integrity at its beginning and end; Potgieter reads this framing and the poem’s balanced structure as wisdom influence alongside its cultic imagery.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The repeated walking motif and the poem’s structure can be observed in the text. Potgieter argues for sapiential influence but notes that Psalm 26 is commonly classified as cultic; the record does not adopt her proposed Persian-period date.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Brings the poem’s ethical “way” language into view alongside its altar and temple imagery, rather than allowing one genre label to predetermine its reading.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The speaker opens and closes by describing a walk in integrity, asks YHWH to test heart and kidneys, distinguishes from violent company, and declares love for YHWH’s house and altar. The poem is not an alphabetic acrostic.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Potgieter argues that the repeated walking motif, concentric structure, and language shared with Israelite wisdom traditions make sapiential influence visible in a poem often classified as cultic. Her proposal offers a way to read ethical conduct and temple imagery together. The present text does not establish a precise performance setting or the Persian-period date proposed in the article.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A first-person prayer declares integrity, distinguishes the speaker from violent company, and expresses attachment to YHWH’s house and altar.
temporal_scope.notes: Wisdom influence is Potgieter’s literary interpretation. Her Persian-period dating proposal is not adopted here.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The integrity motif at both ends and the temple imagery in the central movement support the structural question.

evidence_items.title: Sea and deep imagery under YHWH’s control in Psalm 33:6–9
evidence_items.description: Psalm 33:7 pairs the sea with the deep and depicts both as gathered and stored; Stoltz reads the parallel as a poetic claim about YHWH’s sovereignty over all waters and proposes creation and Exodus resonances.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The sea/deep parallel and the images of gathering and storehouses are in the text. A master’s dissertation argues for several creation and salvation allusions and records a Job 38 alternative; no direct borrowing from a specific ancient myth is asserted.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how a compact water image can carry creation and deliverance associations while keeping a modern reconstruction distinct from the poem’s explicit wording.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 33:6–9 pairs YHWH’s word and breath in creation with the sea gathered like a heap and the deep placed in storehouses; the surrounding lines say that YHWH spoke and it came to be.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Stoltz reads the parallel sea and deep as a merism for all waters under YHWH’s control and argues that the image may recall creation, the Reed Sea, and entry into Canaan. He notes a competing comparison with Job 38’s containment of the sea. These are literary resonances proposed in a master’s dissertation, not proof of dependence on Ugaritic poetry or a date for Psalm 33.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A hymn praises YHWH’s word, creative action, and governance of waters and nations.
temporal_scope.notes: Stoltz’s creation, Exodus, and land-entry resonances are attributed proposals. The dissertation’s broader dating argument is not adopted.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: These verses contain the word-and-water imagery and the creation/deliverance question addressed by the study.

evidence_items.title: The refrain and stanza structure of Psalm 43
evidence_items.description: Psalm 43 has no separate superscription and ends with a refrain also heard twice in Psalm 42; reading the sequence as a three-stanza poem is a literary proposal.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The lack of a heading and repeated refrain are directly observable. Simango reads Psalms 42–43 together as a unified lament, while literary unity does not prove whether the poems were first composed as one piece.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Makes the poem’s repeated movement from petition to hope visible while avoiding a claim about its original compositional history or an unsupported cross-passage route.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 43 has no separate superscription and closes with the same refrain about the downcast soul and hope in God that occurs twice immediately before it in Psalm 42. Its five verses form a short petition followed by renewed praise and hope.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Simango reads Psalms 42–43 as a unified individual lament divided into three stanzas by the shared refrain. He also notes that some ancient manuscript copies reportedly do not separate the two poems, citing Gerald H. Wilson rather than identifying particular witnesses. This item rests on the observable heading and refrain; it does not treat the manuscript report as independently verified or settle whether the poems were originally one composition. No cross-passage relationship edge is authored.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A petitioner asks for vindication and renewed access to God’s holy mountain, with the refrain returning at the poem’s close.
temporal_scope.notes: Literary unity and original single-composition status are distinct questions. Simango’s manuscript note is secondary reporting and is not used as a primary witness claim.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The complete five-verse poem contains the heading status, petition, and closing refrain.

evidence_items.title: Wisdom, wealth, death, and poetic focus in Psalm 49
evidence_items.description: Psalm 49 calls its hearers to attend to a wisdom saying about wealth and death; Pleins argues that the poem’s chiastic structure focuses its teaching on wisdom and endurance.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The article’s accessible abstract states the chiastic interpretation and high-level themes, but the full article was not consulted. The item does not infer a systematic doctrine of the afterlife from this abstract-only source.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Helps readers see the poem’s wisdom argument about wealth and mortality without treating a brief abstract as a settled account of Israelite beliefs about the afterlife.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The poem addresses all peoples, announces a wisdom saying, warns against trusting wealth, and contrasts mortal human status with God’s power to redeem from Sheol.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Pleins argues in the abstract that Psalm 49’s chiastic form focuses its wisdom on wealth, death, and endurance: accumulated wealth cannot prevent death, while divine action—not human wealth—provides protection. Since the full article was inaccessible, the precise strophic map and disputed language about the grave are not reconstructed here, and no settled account of Israelite afterlife belief is inferred.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A public wisdom address challenges hearers who fear the wealthy and asks what human wealth can accomplish in the face of death.
temporal_scope.notes: The chiastic reading is reported from Pleins’s abstract only. The poem’s difficult statements about Sheol and redemption require fuller text-critical and scholarly review.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The full wisdom address develops the relation among listening, wealth, mortality, and divine action.

evidence_items.title: The ten-nation coalition and historical limits in Psalm 83
evidence_items.description: Psalm 83’s enemy list includes Assyria and presents a ten-nation coalition; Mitchell reads the list as an archetypal or eschatological image rather than a secure report of one historical alliance.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The listed peoples and Assyria appear in the poem. Mitchell’s argument that the expanded list and ten-nation motif point beyond a single Jehoshaphat-era coalition is an attributed thesis proposal, not an independently established date or event.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Prevents the enemy list from being treated as a documentary roster of a named war while showing how a later audience might read familiar foes as an archetypal coalition.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The poem names multiple neighboring peoples as a coalition against Israel and includes Assyria in the list. It does not name a date, ruler, battle, or treaty.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Mitchell notes that some names may recall earlier conflict traditions but argues that the ten-nation list, especially its inclusion of Assyria, is difficult to reduce to one local alliance from Jehoshaphat’s time. In his canonical reading, the coalition is archetypal and eschatological. This is Mitchell’s interpretation in a PhD thesis; the poem alone does not establish that date, a specific historical coalition, or a precise eschatological timetable. No cross-passage relationship is authored.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and original setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A communal plea portrays a broad coalition of Israel’s enemies seeking to erase the people and their name.
temporal_scope.notes: Mitchell’s archetypal/eschatological reading is an attributed canonical interpretation. No named conflict or composition date is established here.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The complete petition provides the coalition list and the appeal whose historical referent is debated.

evidence_items.title: Roaring waters and the stream that gladdens the city in Psalm 46
evidence_items.description: Psalm 46 contrasts waters that threaten stability with a stream that gladdens God's city; Schäder reads the images through the poem's spatial movement toward Zion and its temple.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The contrasting water and city imagery is explicit in the poem. The temple-centered spatial reading is Schäder's literary proposal and does not establish an actual river or historical attack.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Clarifies how the poem uses water imagery to move from instability to the city's confidence in God's presence.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 46:2–5 depicts mountains and waters in upheaval, then names a river whose channels gladden God's city and says God is in its midst.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Schäder reads the contrast spatially: the raging waters and hostile nations belong to a destabilized outside, while the city's stream and divine presence mark Zion as an ordered center. The proposal helps explain the poem's geography but does not identify a physical river or prove a particular cultic setting.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; composition date and historical occasion unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A communal confidence poem imagines creation and nations in turmoil while affirming God's presence in the city.
temporal_scope.notes: The spatial and temple-centered interpretation is attributed to Schäder. The poem does not identify a specific attack, river, or date.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: These verses contain the upheaving waters, city stream, and divine-presence contrast addressed by the study.

evidence_items.title: The Davidic heading as a literary frame for Psalm 56
evidence_items.description: Psalm 56's heading links the prayer to David in Gath; Potgieter reads that heading as a Psalter editorial frame connecting the poem's fear and trust language with the David narrative.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The heading and repeated fear/trust language are observable. The proposed editorial function is Potgieter's literary interpretation, and the biblical narrative does not independently state that David was seized in Gath.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Helps readers distinguish what the superscription asks them to associate from what can be independently established about David's biography.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The superscription associates Psalm 56 with David and his encounter in Gath; the prayer names fear, trust in God, hostile speech, and a promise of praise.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Potgieter treats the superscription as a literary/metatextual cue that invites readers to connect the speaker's fear with David's fear in 1 Samuel 21 and to read the prayer as a model of trust. This is an interpretation of the Psalter's heading, not independent evidence that the event occurred as described or that David composed the poem.

periods: Psalter literary and editorial context; date unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A first-person lament voices persecution and trust; its superscription supplies a David-in-Gath frame.
temporal_scope.notes: No composition date is inferred from the superscription. Potgieter's proposed editorial horizon is not an independently dated event.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The chapter's heading and body together provide the literary frame and fear/trust language under discussion.

evidence_items.title: Complaint, remembered acts, and praise in Psalm 77
evidence_items.description: Psalm 77 moves from distress and complaint through remembered divine action to praise; Kamuwanga notes that the prayer contains no explicit petition and interprets historical memory as a reorientation of the speaker.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The movement across the poem is textually observable and described in the article. The claim that the psalm's historical recital responds to exile is a proposed setting and is not adopted as a date.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how the poem's turn to remembered divine action changes its voice without resolving when or for whom it was composed.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The poem begins with a cry from distress, turns to sustained questions and recollection, and closes by recounting God's way through the waters and the leading of the people.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Kamuwanga describes a lament moving from complaint to confidence and praise and observes that it has no explicit petition. He reads recollection of divine action as a reorientation of the sufferer. His proposed exilic setting and broader chaos imagery are not established by the poem alone and are not treated here as composition history.

periods: Ancient Israelite prayer and poetry; date and community setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A petitioner recalls divine acts and the leading of the people through waters while seeking help in present distress.
temporal_scope.notes: The article proposes an exile-oriented context, but this record reports its formal reading without adopting an exilic composition date or direct borrowing from an ancient chaos myth.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The complete poem contains the complaint, recollection, and closing praise whose movement is analyzed.

evidence_items.title: Protection language and wisdom instruction in Psalm 91
evidence_items.description: Psalm 91's safe-way, protected-foot, and fear imagery overlaps with Proverbs 3; Botha argues that the psalm's present form participates in wisdom instruction and proposes literary influence.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Botha's Hebrew-language comparisons are detailed in a full article, but the direction of literary influence and the editorial history are scholarly reconstructions rather than uncontested facts.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Makes the protective promises legible within Israelite wisdom language while distinguishing literary interpretation from a guarantee that every worshipper avoided danger.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 91 combines images of refuge and shelter with a way protected from stumbling, fear of night terror, and a concluding divine speech promising rescue to the one who calls.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Botha compares the psalm's language of walking safely, protection of the foot, and freedom from fear with Proverbs 3. He reads Psalm 91's current form as wisdom-oriented instruction and argues that it also influenced Job 5:17–26. This item records his literary proposal without treating dependence direction, a temple origin, or a date as settled.

periods: Ancient Israelite wisdom and Psalter composition; chronology unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A wisdom-shaped prayer or instruction portrays refuge in YHWH through alternating voices of trust and assurance.
temporal_scope.notes: Botha's Proverbs and Job relationships are attributed literary proposals; the psalm's superscription does not provide a historical date.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The complete poem contains the refuge, way, danger, and concluding assurance language compared with wisdom instruction.

evidence_items.title: The central confession of order in Psalm 92
evidence_items.description: Tucker identifies the poem's central monocolon as its structural and rhetorical pivot and reads its creation imagery as a confession that YHWH orders the world; proposed chiastic schemes are not necessary to this reading.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The placement of the central line and creation language are observable; the claim that they shape an ordered-world confession is Tucker's literary interpretation, while his exile setting remains a proposal.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how the poem answers apparent disorder by placing its confession about YHWH at the center of its praise.
evidence_items.primary_observation: In the Masoretic poem, a short confession about YHWH's exaltation stands at its center, framed by praise for steadfast love, creation, and the flourishing of the righteous.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Tucker counts seven couplets/triplets on either side of the central monocolon and argues that this placement reinforces the confession that YHWH orders the world. He links the poem's creation imagery and Sabbath superscription to that claim, but cautions against forced chiastic readings. His exile-oriented setting is an interpretation, not a secure date.

periods: Ancient Israelite poetry; setting and composition date unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A Sabbath song praises YHWH's acts and contrasts the temporary growth of the wicked with the enduring flourishing of the righteous.
temporal_scope.notes: Tucker's source uses Hebrew numbering that counts the superscription: its central v. 9 is BHF body v. 8. This record does not adopt an exile date or a disputed chiastic arrangement.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The whole song provides its Sabbath label, central confession, creation imagery, and conclusion about the flourishing righteous.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 105 as historical recital in worship: a qualified proposal
evidence_items.description: Gillingham's publisher abstract places Psalms 104–106 in a proposed liturgical collection and argues that historical lessons could be learned through performance; this is a scholarly reconstruction, not independent verification of Psalm 105's narrated events.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Only the publisher abstract and bibliographic page were accessible. The item is restricted to the narrow proposal stated there and does not claim to have consulted the full article.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Offers a source-attributed way to ask how a recitation of ancestral and exodus traditions could function in communal worship.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 105 addresses a worshipping audience and recounts divine action from ancestral promises through the exodus and settlement traditions as grounds for praise and remembrance.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Gillingham's abstract proposes that Psalms 104–106 form a liturgical collection and that historical recollection in Psalms 105–106 enabled participation in Second Temple worship and teaching through song. Because the full article was not accessible, this item attributes only that abstract-level proposal and does not treat the psalm as an independent historical source for each event it narrates.

periods: Psalter collection and proposed Second Temple liturgical reception; date of Psalm 105 unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A praise poem recounts YHWH's dealings with the ancestors and Israel as a basis for communal remembrance.
temporal_scope.notes: Gillingham's article is dated to HeBAI volume 4 (2015), though its publisher page says it was published online in 2018. Only the publisher abstract was inspected; Second Temple liturgical function is an attributed proposal.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The full psalm's historical recital and calls to remember/praise are the subject of the publisher abstract's proposal.

evidence_items.title: Alphabetic form and complete praise in Psalm 111
evidence_items.description: Psalm 111's Masoretic text is a complete alphabetic acrostic; Prinsloo notes that this graphic form may reflect scribal and wisdom-school practices but cannot by itself identify a particular school or date.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The alphabetic sequence is textually observable. Its proposed social setting in scribal and wisdom schools is explicitly probabilistic and is not treated as proof of a date or institution.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Connects a visible poetic technique with a qualified question about writing and learning in the communities that shaped the Psalter.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 111's ten lines proceed through the Hebrew alphabet and praise YHWH's works, righteousness, and covenant faithfulness.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Prinsloo describes Psalms 111 and 112 as complete colon-based alphabetic acrostics and argues that the graphic technique probably presumes a culture of writing and reading, perhaps associated with scribal and wisdom schools. This is a qualified social inference from form, not evidence for a specific school, date, or original performance setting.

periods: Ancient Hebrew poetic and scribal traditions; date unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: An alphabetic hymn recounts YHWH's works and calls the worshipper to praise and fear YHWH.
temporal_scope.notes: The acrostic observation concerns the Masoretic form. The proposed scribal-school context is attributed to Prinsloo and is not independently dated.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The complete alphabetic poem is the evidence for the formal observation and the attributed scribal-context proposal.

evidence_items.title: The imprecation and interpretive ambiguity of Psalm 139
evidence_items.description: Psalm 139 shifts in vv. 19–22 to hostile language about the wicked; Firth proposes that this section can be read as part of a unified prayer of the accused whose ambiguity addresses both innocent and guilty worshippers.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The shift in tone and the integrity debate are well documented. Firth's unified reading is a specific interpretive proposal among disputed alternatives, not a settled solution to the interpolation question.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Explains why the poem's closing appeal for searching may follow an imprecation and why readers disagree about how the sections cohere.
evidence_items.primary_observation: After describing divine knowledge and presence, Psalm 139:19–22 asks God to oppose the wicked and expresses the speaker's hatred of those who hate God; vv. 23–24 then ask God to search and lead the speaker.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Firth notes the live dispute over whether vv. 19–22 belong to the original poem and proposes a unified reading as a prayer of the accused. On this account, deliberate ambiguity allows innocent and guilty worshippers to hear the searching and imprecation differently. The article offers a reading, not proof that the integrity question is settled.

periods: Ancient Israelite prayer and poetry; composition and setting unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A worshipper asks to be searched and known by God after describing divine knowledge and calling for judgment against the wicked.
temporal_scope.notes: Firth's unity proposal is distinguished from alternatives that treat vv. 19–22 as secondary. No date, historical accused person, or original courtroom setting is asserted.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: These closing verses contain the imprecation, the shift in tone, and the concluding request to be searched and led.

evidence_items.title: Illness lament and delayed retribution in Psalm 39
evidence_items.description: Psalm 39 joins restraint of speech and a plea for relief with reflection on the brevity of human life. Botha argues that its illness-lament form carries a wisdom meditation on frustration with delayed retribution, while other readings retain a more direct illness setting.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The poem's wording and movement are directly observable. The larger literary and historical explanation is an attributed scholarly interpretation and remains open to alternatives.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Helps readers notice the tension between the poem's lament-like form and its reflection on mortality and the failure of expected outcomes.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The speaker resolves to guard his speech while the wicked are present, describes human life as fleeting, and asks YHWH to turn his gaze away so he may smile again before he dies.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Botha reads the poem as a wisdom reflection on the apparent delay of retribution, in dialogue with the confident expectations of Psalms 34 and 37. He argues that the form of an individual illness supplication serves that reflection rather than documenting a specific sick person's cultic prayer. Other scholars read the illness language more directly, so the setting remains disputed.

periods: Ancient Israelite wisdom and prayer; composition date unresolved
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A first-person prayer reflects on mortality, divine discipline, and the speaker's frustration; no identifiable historical illness episode is established.
temporal_scope.notes: Botha proposes a late post-exilic literary horizon, but chronology and the poem's relation to other wisdom texts remain scholarly reconstructions and are not adopted as a date.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The full poem contains the speech restraint, mortality reflection, complaint, and petition discussed by Botha. His article numbers the superscription as v. 1; this anchor uses BHF's body-verse numbering.

evidence_items.title: From inspected city to remembered space in Psalm 48
evidence_items.description: The poem invites hearers to inspect Zion's towers, rampart, and buildings after describing the defeat of hostile kings. Steiner proposes that an exilic redaction reframes this confidence through memory and narration after Jerusalem's destruction.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The poem's wording and movement are directly observable. The larger literary and historical explanation is an attributed scholarly interpretation and remains open to alternatives.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how the poem's invitation to look at the city's structures can function as a claim about divine protection while keeping the proposed exilic rereading distinct from archaeological evidence.
evidence_items.primary_observation: After recalling what the community has heard and seen, Psalm 48 directs hearers to walk around Zion, count its towers, and consider its rampart and buildings before telling the next generation.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Steiner distinguishes a proposed earlier layer that grounds confidence in the city's apparent security from an exilic layer that turns this physical space into a remembered and narrated testimony of divine care. He also notes that scholars propose widely different historical occasions and that the poem does not name one specific attack. The layering is a literary-historical model, not an independently established event sequence.

evidence_items.title: A people created or set apart in Psalm 102
evidence_items.description: A syntactic analysis offers a disputed translation of Psalm 102’s Zion stanza: the people may be described as set apart in a present state rather than as a future-created people.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Van Wolde’s full article was inspected, including its syntax and translation argument. Its reading of ברא as “separate” is explicitly one side of an acknowledged scholarly debate; the item reports her argument rather than presenting the lexical proposal as settled.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The translation changes whether the verse predicts a future population or characterizes Zion’s people in relation to the surrounding nations, affecting how the following call to praise is heard.
evidence_items.primary_observation: In BHF numbering, Psalm 102:18b describes the people who praise Yah; many translations understand the participle from ברא as “created” and supply a future sense. Van Wolde parses the clause as a nominal description and reads the participle as a resulting state.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Van Wolde argues that the syntax of the clause and its present descriptive force favor “a people set apart—it praises Yah,” referring back to Zion’s inhabitants, rather than “a newly created people will praise Yah.” She notes that “create” is the standard interpretation and that the meaning of ברא is debated; her proposal is a translation argument, not a settled lexical consensus.

periods: Poetic description of Zion and its people; the verse’s verbal aspect and translation are disputed
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: The Zion stanza contrasts the petitioner, the city, and other nations; the grammatical reading affects whether the people are newly anticipated or presently characterized.
temporal_scope.notes: The article proposes a translation from Hebrew syntax; it does not date the psalm or identify a specific restoration event.

evidence_items.title: The cave superscription and historical limits of Psalm 142
evidence_items.description: Psalm 142’s cave heading supplies a literary frame but does not identify one recoverable episode in David’s life.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Skinner’s full dissertation discussion of Psalm 142, printed pages 198–200, was inspected. The heading is explicit; selecting one cave event is not warranted by the wording alone.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Separates what the superscription says from later attempts to map it onto a particular narrative episode and explains the proposed literary relation to another cave psalm.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The heading associates Psalm 142 with David and a cave, but the poem itself does not name the cave, pursuer, or episode. Skinner compares its superscription and themes with the cave framing of Psalm 57.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Skinner proposes reading Psalm 142 as a thematic companion to Psalm 57; the cave heading may evoke more than one episode and should not be used to select a single historical event. This is an intertextual and editorial interpretation, not independent verification of a Davidic event.

periods: The heading’s historical reference is disputed; the psalm’s composition date and the identity of any cave episode remain unknown.
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A first-person plea for refuge presented by a heading that locates David in a cave without naming a specific episode.
temporal_scope.notes: Skinner’s companion-psalm reading is attributed. Neither the heading nor the poem independently identifies one historical cave event.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: The complete BHF body of Psalm 142 contains the prayer discussed; the heading is treated as a literary frame, not as a verse anchor.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 143:2 in competing readings of Paul’s argument
evidence_items.description: Scholars agree that Galatians 2:16 echoes the Greek wording of Psalm 143:2, but disagree over the role that wording plays in the logic of Galatians 3:10.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Moore’s publisher abstract and Bachmann’s full open-access response were inspected. Bachmann confirms the wording’s use in Galatians 2:16 while contesting Moore’s proposed logical role for it in Galatians 3:10.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how a later reader’s use of Psalm 143:2 can be studied without treating every proposed connection as settled or indexing an unreviewed cross-passage bridge.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 143:2 confesses that no living person is righteous before God. The Greek wording is taken up in Galatians 2:16c; the question addressed by Moore and Bachmann is whether it also supplies a premise in Paul’s argument in Galatians 3:10.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Moore argues that the confession of universal human sinfulness in Psalm 143:2 informs Paul’s denial of justification by works and his conclusion in Galatians 3:10. Bachmann accepts the wording’s echo in Galatians 2:16c but rejects the premise Moore assigns it in 3:10, arguing that Galatians 3:10–12 uses two syllogisms with premises from Deuteronomy 27:26, Habakkuk 2:4, and Leviticus 18:5. This record preserves the disagreement as later reception and does not create a curated relationship route.

periods: Later Christian reception in Paul’s first-century letter and modern interpretation of its argument; no date for the psalm’s composition is inferred.
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A petition acknowledging human unrighteousness before God, later discussed in relation to Paul’s scriptural argument.
temporal_scope.notes: Moore’s full article was not accessible; his argument is reported from the publisher abstract. Bachmann’s full response is accessible in German. The dispute concerns the logical role in Galatians 3:10, not whether the wording is echoed in Galatians 2:16c.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: This is the wording later discussed by Moore and Bachmann; the CKL anchor remains on Psalm 143 and does not create a cross-passage route.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 144 as a dependent royal victory song
evidence_items.description: Psalm 144’s royal battle language is read by Zenger as a supplication in which the king’s victory depends on YHWH’s rescue.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The publisher-hosted article content at footnote 50 and its accompanying discussion was inspected. Zenger’s reading is explicit there; its proposed editorial relations remain an interpretation, not a historical battle identification.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Explains how a royal victory song can emphasize human dependence and divine rescue rather than autonomous royal power, while keeping the proposed literary setting distinct from a known campaign.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 144 combines a royal speaker trained for battle, a meditation on human frailty, and a request for rescue. Zenger identifies it as the final royal psalm before Psalm 145 and interprets its relation to Psalm 18 as a shift from victory thanksgiving to supplication.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Zenger argues that Psalm 144 rereads Psalm 18: the king wins only because YHWH rescues him. He also sees the poem’s anthropology as lowering the king from divine status while leaving him the object of divine care and service. These are attributed final-form proposals; the psalm does not identify a specific historical battle.

periods: Final-form and redactional interpretation in Book V of the Psalter; no composition date or historical campaign is established.
temporal_scope.narrative_setting: A royal prayer links battle, human frailty, and deliverance within the final arrangement before Psalm 145.
temporal_scope.notes: The relation to Psalm 18 and the broader royal-psalm arrangement are Zenger’s interpretations. Only his directly visible footnote argument is used; the publisher marks the full article as access-restricted.

scripture_references.relevance_rationale: These verses introduce the royal speaker, battle training, and meditation on human frailty discussed in Zenger’s reading.

evidence_items.passage_relevance: Makes the poem’s shifts of speaker and addressee a question readers can examine instead of treating its movement from petition to confidence as one undifferentiated utterance.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 4 moves among speech addressed to YHWH, speech about YHWH, and direct address to human hearers; its closing confidence follows this sequence of changing discourse positions.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Leite’s abstract describes a poetic, macro-structural, and dialogic analysis and proposes that stanza divisions follow inflected-person shifts. It calls this a dialogue among three cosmic figures; the accessible abstract does not identify them, so no identities are supplied here.

evidence_items.title: Contentment in YHWH as Psalm 16’s wisdom teaching
evidence_items.description: Botha reads Psalm 16 as a Torah-wisdom composition that presents well-being as contentment in YHWH’s presence and guidance, within the Psalms 15-24 cluster.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Botha’s full argument and textual analysis were inspected. He explicitly contrasts his wisdom reading with Hossfeld and Zenger’s supplication reading; genre and redaction history remain debated.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how YHWH as portion, counsel, and path can function as instruction about a good life while distinguishing editorial context from original date.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 16 names YHWH as the speaker’s allotted portion, describes counsel during the night, and closes with the path of life and enduring pleasures in YHWH’s presence.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Botha argues that these features make Psalm 16 a Torah-wisdom teaching composition, structurally and theologically related to Psalms 1, 19, and 23 within Psalms 15-24. He contrasts this with Hossfeld and Zenger’s interpretation as an individual supplication; his collection-history proposal is not treated as established chronology.

periods: Literary context of the Psalter; no specific historical event or composition date established

temporal_scope.notes: Botha’s wisdom genre and Psalter-redaction claims are interpretations; the article records a competing supplication reading and disputed dating.

evidence_items.title: The distinctive opening line in Psalm 18 and its Samuel parallel
evidence_items.description: Lee compares the opening “I love you, YHWH, my strength” line in Psalm 18 with the parallel song in 2 Samuel 22, where the line is absent, and examines the unusual Hebrew verb used there.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The English abstract and final English summary identify the line’s absence from 2 Samuel 22 and say its qal form of rhm is otherwise unique in the Hebrew Bible. The detailed analysis is in Korean and was not independently assessed; editorial modernization is reported as a proposal.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows that the parallel song is not mechanically identical in its two biblical placements and that the difference affects translation of the Psalm’s opening.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The Psalm’s opening line uses a qal form of the Hebrew root rhm, commonly rendered “I love you,” and Lee reports that the line does not appear in the parallel song in 2 Samuel 22.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Lee argues that the Psalmic form revises and clarifies the Samuel version and treats the unusual rhm form in light of Aramaic usage and Psalm 116. This is his linguistic/editorial reconstruction; the accessible English summary does not permit independent review of the Korean analysis.

evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The publisher abstract explicitly states the hospitality context and proposed translation. The full article was not accessible, so its lexical argument and alternatives remain to be checked.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Clarifies how the host-and-guest scene may shape the final line’s sense of movement and expectation, while identifying “return” as a proposal.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 23:5-6 moves from a prepared table, anointed head, and overflowing cup to a statement about the speaker’s future in YHWH’s house.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Arterbury and Bellinger argue that the host image is best understood against ancient hospitality customs and that this reading supports “I shall return to the house of the Lord.” The abstract is the accessible source; no consensus or exclusive translation is claimed.

evidence_items.title: “Reflect” rather than inspect an offering in Psalm 27:4
evidence_items.description: Botha reads בקר as reflection within YHWH’s temple presence, rather than a priest’s inspection of an offering, in light of the verse’s parallelism and Psalms 25-34.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Botha’s open-access article, translation, immediate argument, and cluster parallels were inspected. His reading contests an earlier cultic proposal; the verb and reconstructed cultic alternatives remain debated.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Makes the Hebrew verb in the psalmist’s “one thing” request visible and lets readers compare it with the parallel gaze language and the poem’s repeated desire for YHWH’s presence.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 27:4 pairs the desire to gaze on YHWH’s kindness with בקר in the phrase about YHWH’s temple; later lines repeat the desire to seek YHWH’s face and see divine goodness.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Botha argues that בקר should mean reflecting in the temple, as communion and Torah-related meditation, rather than inspecting a sacrificial offering or practicing divination. He bases the reading on parallelism, the two-part structure, and links with Psalms 16, 23, and 25-34.

evidence_items.description: Töyräänvuori proposes comparing Psalm 29 not only with the Baal Cycle (KTU 1.4 VII 25-52) but also with Baal’s enthronement hymn (KTU 1.101) and Syrian storm-god imagery.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The peer-reviewed article’s publisher abstract and record were inspected; the full argument is restricted. They verify the comparative method, not a specific borrowing claim or the outcome of the comparison.

evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 29 depicts YHWH’s voice over waters and in thunder and names Lebanon, Sirion, and wilderness in its storm poem; this imagery has prompted Ugaritic comparisons.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Töyräänvuori proposes triangulating Psalm 29 with the Baal Cycle, the separate Baal enthronement hymn KTU 1.101, and Syrian glyptic depictions. The abstract supports the method only; it does not establish direct literary dependence, an original Baal hymn, or a composition date.

evidence_items.title: Entrusting spirit and time to YHWH’s hand
evidence_items.description: Psalm 31 places the speaker’s spirit and times in YHWH’s hand while using the hand of enemies for danger; Botha reads it as testimony of trust within Psalms 25-34.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Botha’s full article and text table were inspected, including the paired hand expressions and cluster argument. The post-exilic social setting is an attributed reconstruction; no historical opponent or date is identified.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The repeated “hand” language links trust and danger and helps explain why a prayer mixing distress and thanksgiving can exhort a community.
evidence_items.primary_observation: The speaker commits the spirit to YHWH’s hand and later says the speaker’s times are in that hand; the poem contrasts this with the enemy’s hand and hidden nets.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Botha reads Psalm 31 within Psalms 25-34 as a testimony of rescue that encourages a community to trust YHWH. He argues that the cluster’s central conflict is ethical and social, between humble and poor worshippers and arrogant persecutors in post-exilic Judah; this setting is his reconstruction.

evidence_items.title: Confession and guidance as parallel stanzas in Psalm 32
evidence_items.description: Potgieter reads Psalm 32 as two linked stanzas: the first moves from blessing through silence to confession, and the second from refuge to divine instruction and a call for the righteous to rejoice.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Potgieter’s full open-access analysis was inspected, including its Hebrew stichometric table, repeated keywords, proposed two-stanza structure, and note on alternative growth models. The structural conclusion is attributed, not consensus.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: Shows how repeated language connects the personal confession in vv. 1-5 with instruction and communal exhortation in vv. 6-11.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 32 repeats forgiveness and sin language in vv. 1-5 and links vv. 6-11 through repetitions about protection, joy, and the righteous; v. 8 shifts into direct instruction.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Potgieter proposes a unified wisdom composition in two stanzas, 1-5 and 6-11, each with three corresponding strophes. He reads confession and acceptance of YHWH’s guidance as one pedagogical movement. He notes alternatives that posit a thanksgiving core with later wisdom framing, so the compositional conclusion is disputed.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 34’s teacher-student address and wisdom rhetoric
evidence_items.description: Psalm 34 shifts from praise to direct instruction: the speaker calls “children” to listen and learn the fear of YHWH. Brown compares this rhetoric with Proverbs while declining to treat “wisdom psalm” as a settled genre label.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The chapter excerpt and publication record were inspected, but the full chapter was inaccessible. The record is limited to the excerpt’s explicit framing and is not a full account of Brown’s argument.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The shift from first-person praise to instruction helps readers notice a teaching voice without assuming a formal school setting or settled wisdom-psalm category.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 34:11-14 (BHF numbering) addresses hearers as children, invites them to listen, and teaches the fear of YHWH through instructions about speech, peace, and life.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Brown compares Psalm 34’s address and instruction with Proverbs and argues that shared wisdom rhetoric can be studied without classifying the whole poem as a “wisdom psalm.” The chapter’s accessible excerpt explicitly treats that genre label as methodologically unsettled.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 40’s rescue prayer reused in 4Q160
evidence_items.description: Jassen compares 4Q160 (Samuel Apocryphon) 3–5 ii 1–4 with Psalm 40:2–4 and reads the psalm’s remembered rescue and present petition as literary units that the later composition combines into one prayer.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: Only the peer-reviewed article’s publisher abstract and bibliographic record were accessible. The record states only the abstract’s specific comparison and does not claim that 4Q160 is a manuscript witness to the wording of Psalm 40.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: This gives readers a concrete example of a Second Temple Jewish composition reusing a psalm as a literary model, while distinguishing reception history from evidence for the psalm’s original wording.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 40:2-4 recounts being drawn from danger and given a new song; Jassen identifies language and structure in this passage as a model used in 4Q160 3–5 ii 1–4.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Jassen argues that Psalm 40 moves from remembered divine aid to a current petition, whereas the author of 4Q160 combines those functions in one prayer while retaining language and structure from Psalm 40:2–4. This is a proposal about later literary reuse, not a claim that 4Q160 preserves a variant biblical reading.

The accessible abstract does not supply the full marker-by-marker case.

evidence_items.title: Psalm 78’s historical recital as instruction
evidence_items.description: Kim and van Rooy divide Psalm 78 into an introduction (vv. 1–8) and two recitals (vv. 9–39 and 40–72), describing its genre as mixed historical and didactic poetry.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The complete open-access article was inspected. Its proposed structure and genre are explicitly presented alongside the article’s account of substantial scholarly disagreement over Psalm 78’s divisions, genre, date, and setting.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The proposed divisions help readers follow how a call to teach memory becomes two recitals of Israel’s past, without turning the poem into a neutral chronicle or dating its composition from the events it recounts.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Psalm 78:1-8 addresses hearers and calls the coming generation to learn; vv. 9-72 recount episodes of Israel’s history through repeated patterns of failure, divine response, and remembered provision.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Kim and van Rooy propose an introduction in vv. 1-8 followed by two historical-didactic recitals in vv. 9-39 and 40-72. They explicitly note that scholars disagree over the Psalm’s structure, genre, date, and setting, with proposals ranging from the tenth century to the postexilic period; this item assigns no composition date.

temporal_scope.notes: The article explicitly reports a wide range of scholarly proposals about date and Sitz im Leben; no one date or performance context is adopted here.
